body.text: Overview and Empirical Foundations of Rett syndrome

Rett syndrome (RTT) is a genetic disorder that typically becomes apparent after 6, 18 months of age in girls. Symptoms include impairments in language and coordination, and repetitive movements. Those affected often have slower growth, difficulty walking, and a smaller head size. Complications can include seizures, scoliosis, and sleeping problems. The severity of the condition, however, is variable.

Rett syndrome is due to a genetic mutation, with around 90% of cases in the MECP2 gene, on the X chromosome (specifically Xq28). It almost always occurs as a new mutation, with less than one percent of cases being inherited. It occurs almost exclusively in girls, boys who have a similar mutation typically die shortly after birth. Diagnosis is based on the symptoms and can be confirmed with genetic testing.

There is no known consistent cure for Rett syndrome. Treatment is directed at improving symptoms. The strongest FDA approved contender is trofinetide (Daybue). Anticonvulsants may be used to help with seizures. Special education, physiotherapy, and leg braces may also be useful depending on the needs of the child. Many of those with the condition live into middle age.
